answers.text: Lock the output to three fixed lines in a set order so it can't drift between runs. Define each line exactly — time only, pallet count alone, damage or 'none' — no overlap between lines.
Specify the list structure exactly: one line per call, fixed fields, a follow-up flag on each. State that the follow-up count is derived by summing the flagged entries, not asserted separately.

There's an internal inconsistency in how the visit's timing is described. Starting 8am for a six-hour job finishes around 2pm on the 22nd itself, not the 23rd as stated. It comes down to the finish date disagreeing with its own arithmetic — six hours doesn't reach the next day.
Recalculating, 96 to 118 comes out at about 23%, not the stated 20%. Run separately, 9 out of 118 late gives about 92% on-time — that figure holds up.

Output 2 is the one to approve, since the number is derived, not asserted. Output 1 leaves out the two figures behind the percentage — total tickets and SLA closures. Output 1's figure isn't necessarily wrong, only unconfirmable without an independent re-count.
I'd send Email 2 without further checking — it cites the volume figures and PO log. The claim in Email 1 that can't be checked is the rate expectation itself; nothing supports it.

I'd treat the rates and retainer cap as sensitive by default — redact or confirm the tool's vetted first. Because the NDA clause names both the client and us, it gets the same caution as the pricing.
I'd add a named cross-cast step: recompute the month's stock totals independently and compare. That check sits right before the reconciliation reaches finance, not earlier in the process.

An error at extraction doesn't stay contained; it propagates through the PO match and approval note. The automatic-submission step is the point of no return; that's specifically where the gate belongs.
